# ANN benchmark and index updates

<!-- Generated by `make ann` (ml/ann/run.py). Do not edit by hand. -->

SASRec retrieval scores the user vector against every item vector with an in-process
FAISS index and returns the top items. With 3,459 items that is an exact `IndexFlatIP`
search. This report asks (1) at what catalog size exact search should give way to an
approximate (ANN) index and how to set its parameters, and (2) how to keep an index
current while items are added and removed. Item vectors are synthetic stand-ins with
the cluster structure of the real catalog (64-d, like SASRec's), scaled to 100K and 1M
items.

## Summary

- **Flat** costs about 3.7 ns per item per query on one core: 36 µs at 3,459, 389 µs at 100K, 3.64 ms at 1M (P50). At 1M items its P99 (4.33 ms) still fits the 35 ms retrieval budget, but each query takes 3.71 ms of CPU, about 135 queries/s per core at 50% utilization.
- **When to switch**: once Flat needs more than ~1 ms of CPU per query (≈250K items at 64-d), use an ANN index; below that Flat is exact, has no parameters and no training, and adding an item is an append. The current catalog (3,459 items) stays on Flat.
- **Recall@100 ≥ 0.95** at 1M: IVF-Flat (nlist 4096, nprobe 32) with P99 96 µs, 265 MB, recall 0.967 (5th percentile over users 0.86).
- **Recall@100 ≥ 0.99** at 1M: IVF-Flat (nlist 4096, nprobe 64) with P99 152 µs, 265 MB, recall 0.995 (5th percentile over users 0.97).
- **IVF vs HNSW at k = 100** (1M items): for recall ≥ 0.95 IVF-Flat's P99 is 96 µs against HNSW's 300 µs; for recall ≥ 0.99 IVF-Flat needs P99 152 µs, while no HNSW setting in the sweep gets there (best 0.9899 at M 64, efC 200, efSearch 1024, P99 2.00 ms). HNSW's shortfall is a tail that more search does not remove: at M 64, efC 200, efSearch 1024, 1.6% of users still get recall below 0.9; their exact top-100 spans a median of 2 categories against 1 for all users, i.e. they sit between clusters. IVF's coarse step probes cells on both sides: at nlist 4096, nprobe 64, 0.8% of users are below 0.9.
- **Top-200** (what the retrieval stage asks for), 1M items: for recall@200 ≥ 0.99, IVF-Flat gets there at the same nprobe 64 as for top-100 (P99 162 µs vs 169 µs); HNSW gets there at the same efSearch 2048 as for top-100 (P99 4.88 ms vs 4.92 ms), slower than exact search (Flat P99 4.71 ms).
- **IVF with new categories added incrementally**: after 300,000 new-category items the inverted lists' imbalance factor went from 1.05 to 5.52 (largest list 2.4x → 68.4x the mean). New-category users compare 4.4x as many vectors as on a rebuilt index (P99 330 µs vs 97 µs) and get recall 0.841 / 0.24 instead of 0.947 / 0.81 (mean / P5). A full rebuild of 1,000,000 items takes 23.9 s and brings the imbalance back to 1.05.
- **HNSW** keeps its recall as items are added: after the last batch 0.966 / 0.969 (old / new-category users) vs 0.967 / 0.971 for a graph built from scratch (24.1 s). It cannot delete, and filtering deleted items at search time holds up only when deletions are scattered: with 50% of the items deleted at random, recall is 0.965 / 0.91 (rebuilt: 0.973 / 0.96); deleting whole categories (10% of the items) drops it to 0.893 / 0.01, and a rebuild (20.9 s) restores 0.957 / 0.79.
- **In production**: add new items to the serving index as they arrive, rebuild from scratch on a schedule (and when the list imbalance or the golden-query recall crosses a threshold), and ship each rebuilt index as a new bundle version: load it next to the current one, check golden-query recall against exact search, switch atomically, keep the old version for rollback.

## Vectors

1. **Real vectors.** MiniOneRec's text embeddings of the 3,459 Office items (`third_party/MiniOneRec/data/Amazon/index/Office_Products.emb-qwen-td.npy`, 3,459 x 2,560, SHA-256 `0aa6ad769935e6e1...`) are L2-normalized, centered and reduced to 64 dimensions by PCA (74.6% of the variance; the 64 components' participation ratio is 17 effective dimensions), then normalized again.
2. **Mixture.** A Gaussian mixture with full covariances is fitted to them by EM (k-means start). The number of components and the covariance regularization (added to the diagonal) are chosen by 5-fold cross-validated log-likelihood: **64 components, regularization 0.001**. Component weights range from 0.003 to 0.036.
3. **Synthetic catalogs** of any size are drawn from the mixture and L2-normalized (inner product = cosine). Each item's component plays the role of its category.
4. **Users.** A user has a history of 1 to 10 items (uniform). Each history item comes from the user's home category with probability 0.7, otherwise from anywhere in the catalog; the user vector is the recency-weighted sum (weight 0.8 per step back) of the history's item vectors, normalized.

Cross-validated log-likelihood per item (higher is better):

| components | reg 0.0005 | reg 0.001 | reg 0.002 | reg 0.004 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16 | 91.1 | 90.5 | 86.9 | 79.8 |
| 32 | 92.5 | 94.3 | 91.0 | 83.3 |
| 64 | 86.9 | **95.0** | 93.7 | 86.0 |
| 128 | 75.9 | 92.9 | 94.8 | 87.7 |

How close neighbours are, real vs. synthetic at the same size (3,459 items): cosine to the r-th nearest other item, 10th / 50th / 90th percentile over items.

| r | real | synthetic |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.82 / 0.94 / 0.99 | 0.77 / 0.85 / 0.90 |
| 10 | 0.64 / 0.84 / 0.93 | 0.66 / 0.77 / 0.84 |
| 100 | 0.36 / 0.56 / 0.73 | 0.35 / 0.53 / 0.70 |

The 100th-neighbour similarities match, which is the scale recall@100 works at. The
real catalog has closer nearest neighbours (near-duplicate listings and variants of
one product) that the mixture does not reproduce: within a component, synthetic
items are spread evenly, so neighbourhoods are less distinct than in real data and
the synthetic catalogs are, if anything, harder for an ANN index. The real and the
synthetic 3,459-item catalogs are both benchmarked below as a check.

| Catalog | Items | Source | Queries | Vector digest |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| real | 3,459 | real PCA vectors | 2,000 | `02022eb8b69802c0` |
| synthetic | 3,459 | mixture draw | 2,000 | `aea9e0e79a28abea` |
| 100K | 100,000 | mixture draw | 2,000 | `8102e0b50b5b2049` |
| 1M | 1,000,000 | mixture draw | 2,000 | `6d084c83e7e1a26f` |

Check: over the 32 IVF and HNSW settings run on both 3,459-item catalogs, recall@100 on the synthetic catalog is within 0.030 of the real one (mean difference +0.002), so the mixture reproduces how hard the real vectors are for these indexes at this size.

## When to switch from Flat

The retrieval stage has 35 ms of the request's 100 ms deadline, and that includes encoding the user's history. Flat search is a single pass over all vectors, so its cost grows linearly with the catalog:

| Catalog | Flat P50 | Flat P99 | Mean (= CPU per query) | P99 / 35 ms | Queries/s per core at 50% |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| real (3,459) | 35 µs | 42 µs | 35 µs | 0.1% | 14,131 |
| synthetic (3,459) | 36 µs | 42 µs | 36 µs | 0.1% | 13,768 |
| 100K (100,000) | 389 µs | 434 µs | 391 µs | 1.2% | 1,278 |
| 1M (1,000,000) | 3.64 ms | 4.33 ms | 3.71 ms | 12.4% | 135 |

A linear fit over the synthetic sizes gives 23 µs + 3.68 ns per item (mean) and 4.31 ns per item at P99. Latency alone would allow millions of items: P99 reaches 10 ms at about 2.5M items. The limit is CPU: every request pays the full scan, and the model-server has a few cores. Largest catalog that keeps Flat's CPU per query within a budget:

| CPU per query | Queries/s per core at 50% | Largest Flat catalog |
|---|---|---|
| 250 µs | 2,000 | 60K |
| 500 µs | 1,000 | 150K |
| 1.00 ms | 500 | 250K |
| 2.00 ms | 250 | 550K |
| 5.00 ms | 100 | 1.5M |

These are service times of single queries; under concurrent load, queueing adds to them, which is another reason to keep per-query CPU small.

With ~1 ms per query as the limit (a few hundred requests/s per core), switch to ANN at roughly 250K items; below that Flat is exact, needs no training or tuning, and a new item is just appended. The current catalog (3,459 items, 35 µs per query) stays on Flat.

How the parameters behave:

- IVF at 100K: nlist 1024 (≈ 3 √n) with nprobe 32 reaches 0.996 while comparing 3,164 vectors per query (3.2% of the catalog).
- IVF at 1M: nlist 4096 (≈ 4 √n) with nprobe 64 reaches 0.995 while comparing 15,880 vectors per query (1.6% of the catalog).
- IVF nlist at 1M: nlist 1024: trains in 1.6 s, recall ≥ 0.99 at nprobe 32 (P99 230 µs); nlist 4096: trains in 23.7 s, recall ≥ 0.99 at nprobe 64 (P99 152 µs); nlist 16384: trains in 93.4 s, recall ≥ 0.99 at nprobe 256 (P99 397 µs). More lists scan fewer vectors per probe but need more probes for the same recall, and the coarse quantizer (all nlist centroids, scanned on every query) and k-means training grow with nlist. The fastest nlist for recall ≥ 0.99 was ≈ 3 √n at 100K and ≈ 4 √n at 1M (FAISS's guideline is 4√n to 16√n); FAISS wants at least 39 training points per centroid.
- nprobe trades recall for time; latency follows the vectors compared.
- HNSW at 1M: memory M 16: 400 MB, M 32: 528 MB, M 64: 784 MB. efConstruction 40 → 200 costs 8.1 s → 23.4 s of build time and lifts the worst users (P5 recall at efSearch 256: 0.67 → 0.94). efSearch is the query-time knob; FAISS does not raise it to k: with efSearch < k it still returns k items, from a shorter search.
- IVF-PQ at 1M: m 16 (16 bytes per vector, 25 MB) tops out at 0.486, 0.841 with k_factor 4 re-scoring (281 MB); m 32 (32 bytes per vector, 41 MB) tops out at 0.826, 0.999 with k_factor 4 re-scoring (297 MB). PQ's distortion caps recall however many lists are probed; re-scoring PQ candidates with the full vectors (IndexRefineFlat) recovers IVF-Flat's recall but keeps the full vectors in memory, so PQ pays only when memory is the constraint.

## Index updates

The catalog starts with 500,000 items of the old categories and receives 5 batches of 100,000 items; 60% of every batch belongs to new categories: 13 of the mixture components (a random one and its nearest neighbours, 20% of the mixture weight) that the initial catalog does not contain, i.e. a region of the space the initial k-means never saw. A control stream adds old-category batches only. IVF-Flat uses nlist 4096 and nprobe 32; HNSW uses M 32, efConstruction 200, efSearch 256. Queries: 1,000 users of old categories and 1,000 of new ones, scored against the exact top-100 of the catalog at each point.

### HNSW: deletions

`IndexHNSWFlat.remove_ids` raises: deleted items cannot leave the graph. They can be filtered at search time (an `IDSelectorBitmap` of live ids in `SearchParametersHNSW`): the search still walks through deleted nodes but does not return them. Deleting at random (product churn) vs. whole old categories, on the final incrementally built graph, at efSearch 256, at efSearch scaled by 1 / (live share), and after rebuilding a graph on the live items:

| Deleted | Share | Filter: recall | P99 | compared | Scaled: efSearch | recall | P99 | compared | Rebuild: recall | P99 | build |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| random | 10% | 0.967 / 0.93 | 474 µs | 4,846 | 284 | 0.969 / 0.95 | 514 µs | 5,163 | 0.971 / 0.94 | 454 µs | 20.8 s |
| random | 30% | 0.967 / 0.92 | 477 µs | 4,846 | 366 | 0.973 / 0.96 | 650 µs | 6,002 | 0.976 / 0.95 | 429 µs | 14.7 s |
| random | 50% | 0.965 / 0.91 | 479 µs | 4,846 | 512 | 0.977 / 0.97 | 921 µs | 7,261 | 0.973 / 0.96 | 392 µs | 9.3 s |
| category | 10% | 0.893 / 0.01 | 494 µs | 4,846 | 285 | 0.895 / 0.01 | 521 µs | 5,174 | 0.957 / 0.79 | 466 µs | 20.9 s |
| category | 31% | 0.797 / 0.00 | 492 µs | 4,846 | 369 | 0.811 / 0.00 | 671 µs | 6,033 | 0.956 / 0.75 | 462 µs | 15.6 s |
| category | 52% | 0.649 / 0.00 | 541 µs | 4,846 | 531 | 0.672 / 0.00 | 1.06 ms | 7,407 | 0.942 / 0.55 | 518 µs | 11.3 s |

Filtering leaves the walk unchanged: every filtered search compares the same 4,846 vectors whatever share is deleted, so its cost does not depend on the deletions (P99 differences between these rows are measurement noise); what changes is how many of the visited nodes may be returned. Scattered deletions leave live neighbours along the walk. A deleted category is a region where every visited node is dead, so the users whose neighbours were there get almost nothing right (P5 recall near 0), and a larger efSearch does not fix it.

IVF can delete in place: `remove_ids` of 100,000 random ids (10%) from the 1,000,000-item IVF-Flat took 91 ms (it scans every inverted list).

### What this means for serving

- Incremental adds keep an IVF index working but let it decay under drift: new categories land in the few old cells nearest to them, the imbalance factor grows (1.05 → 5.52) and so do the vectors a new-category query compares (3,701 → 35,721; 8,038 on a rebuilt index), while recall for those users stays low (0.841 / 0.24 vs 0.947 / 0.81 rebuilt). The no-drift control stays at 1.05: adding more of the same distribution is harmless; new regions of the space are what the old centroids cannot cover.
- A full IVF rebuild (k-means + add) of 1,000,000 items takes 23.9 s with 4096 lists: cheap enough to run on a schedule (nightly) and on demand. In between, adding a 100,000-item batch to the serving index takes 0.3 s (IVF) or 3.5 s (HNSW).
- Rebuild triggers that are cheap to watch: the imbalance factor of the inverted lists (computed from list sizes, no queries), and recall on a fixed golden query set against exact search.
- HNSW handles additions without retraining; deletions are its weak spot. Scattered deletions can be filtered with an IDSelector (memory and walk stay as large as the original graph) until a scheduled rebuild; removing a whole category needs a rebuild before (or with) the removal. IVF can remove ids in place.
- A rebuilt index is a new version: build it offline next to the serving one, check golden-query recall against Flat, switch the pointer atomically, and keep the previous version loaded for rollback. Items added after the rebuild's snapshot are added to the new index before the switch, so nothing is lost between versions.

## Reproduce

```
make ann                                # this file and artifacts/ann/ann.json
make ann ANN_FLAGS=--preliminary        # same, marked preliminary
python -m ml.ann.run --render-only      # re-render from artifacts/ann/ann.json
```

This run took 20.7 min. The vectors, queries and exact top-k are identical on every run (see the digests); IVF training is seeded. Latency and build times vary with the machine's load, and HNSW graphs built with several threads differ slightly from run to run, so their recall can move in the third decimal.
